papers.t: The leukaemia in pregnancy study, a national multicentre retrospective study of pregnancy outcomes in women with concurrent or historic diagnoses of acute leukaemia
papers.c: Most PAL neonates were born with a normal birthweight and no obstetric complications. For PAL, pregnancy outcomes are comparable to those of the general population.
ab: The leukaemia in pregnancy study was a multicentre retrospective study of pregnancy outcomes of women with concurrent (CAL) or previous (PAL) acute leukaemia. Cases were identified from eight hospitals. Of 39 screened cases, 12 CAL and 21 PAL cases were described, with one belonging to both groups. In the CAL cohort, there were 12 pregnancies with 10 infants delivered, one induced abortion and one unknown outcome. Six of 10 CAL women delivered prior to chemotherapy, two received chemotherapy both antenatally and postnatally, and in two, information was not available. All 10 infants were alive 28 days post-delivery. In the PAL group, 25 pregnancies were identified with 23 deliveries (two with twins), one miscarriage and one with unknown outcomes. Pregnancy complications were reported in four women. Twenty-four of 25 infants were alive 28 days after delivery with one unknown status. Acute leukaemia diagnosed during pregnancy was generally managed with expedited delivery. Neonates born to women with CAL had low birthweights and were premature. Most PAL neonates were born with a normal birthweight and no obstetric complications. For PAL, pregnancy outcomes are comparable to those of the general population.

papers.t: Ultra-Low-Dose Long-Axial-Field-of-View [18F]FDG PET with CT-Free Attenuation Correction for Staging Hodgkin Lymphoma in Pregnancy
Subtype- and functional class-dependent prognostic impact of CSF3R mutations in acute myeloid leukaemia: A cohort study of 2500 patients
papers.c: In CEBPA-bZip AML, both MPM and CTTM showed adverse EFS and RFS associations, although the CTTM subgroup was small. The prognostic impact of CSF3Rmut in AML depends on molecular context and functional mutation class, with the strongest adverse associations observed in CEBPA-bZip AML.
ab: Colony-stimulating factor 3 receptor (CSF3R) mutations occur in acute myeloid leukaemia (AML), but their prognostic significance remains unclear. We analysed 2500 patients with newly diagnosed de novo non-acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APL) AML treated with intensive induction therapy. CSF3Rmut were identified in 3.5% and frequently co-occurred with CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein alpha bZIP domain (CEBPA-bZip) mutations and RUNX family transcription factor 1::RUNX1 partner transcriptional co-repressor 1 (RUNX1::RUNX1T1) fusions. In the entire cohort, CSF3Rmut were associated with inferior relapse-free survival (RFS), but not overall survival (OS) or event-free survival (EFS). The prognostic impact was context-dependent. The adverse association was most consistent in CEBPA-bZip AML, with inferior OS, EFS (hazard ratio [HR], 2.76; p = 0.001) and RFS (HR, 2.66; p = 0.002) and persisted after multivariable adjustment and time-dependent modelling of transplantation. Membrane-proximal activating mutations (MPM) were associated primarily with inferior RFS (HR, 2.27; p = 0.001) in the overall cohort, whereas cytoplasmic-tail truncating mutations (CTTM) showed no consistent adverse effect. In CEBPA-bZip AML, both MPM and CTTM showed adverse EFS and RFS associations, although the CTTM subgroup was small. The prognostic impact of CSF3Rmut in AML depends on molecular context and functional mutation class, with the strongest adverse associations observed in CEBPA-bZip AML.

papers.t: The prognostic impact of CEBPA mutation in acute myeloid leukemia patients undergoing allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation
papers.c: Conversely, the presence of GATA2 mutations showed no benefit. Our findings suggest that CEBPAmut patients with nontypical in-frame shift in bZIP region or with the co-mutation of FLT3-ITD could benefit from allo-HSCT.
ab: The presence of mutations in basic leucine zipper (bZIP) region of the CEBPA gene in patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is defined as a favorable risk marker according to the guidelines. A total of 173 CEBPA-mutated AML patients receiving allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) were retrospectively recruited, compared with 345 control patients selected by propensity score matching. Patients carrying CEBPAmut had a better 5-year PFS than CEBPAwt group (60.8% vs. 55.0%, P = 0.016). Failure to achieve complete remission after first induction chemotherapy, the presence of CEBPA mutation before allo-HSCT and the absence of maintenance therapy were proven to be statistically significant factors for worse survival (all P < 0.001). Surprisingly, survival analysis revealed that patients with nontypical in-frame bZIP mutations or harboring both FLT3-ITD and CEBPA mutations had a favorable outcome of PFS (CEBPAin-frame bZIP 59.9% vs. CEBPAno in-frame bZIP 63.3% vs. CEBPAwt 55.0%, P = 0.045; CEBPAmut/FLT3-ITDmut 75.9% vs. CEBPAmut/FLT3-ITDwt 57.3% vs. CEBPAwt 55.0%, P = 0.02). Conversely, the presence of GATA2 mutations showed no benefit. Our findings suggest that CEBPAmut patients with nontypical in-frame shift in bZIP region or with the co-mutation of FLT3-ITD could benefit from allo-HSCT.

papers.t: External Validation of the CARE-BMT and Modified CARE-BMT Scores for Cardiac Event Prediction After Allogeneic Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation in Acute Myeloid Leukemia
papers.c: In this AML allo-HCT cohort, cardiac events occurred in approximately 7% of patients and were associated with worse survival and increased NRM. Incorporating standard-dose PTCy improved risk stratification, supporting inclusion of transplant-specific variables in cardiovascular risk prediction after allo-HCT.
ab: Background

Cardiac events after allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (allo-HCT) are associated with increased non-relapse mortality (NRM) and inferior survival. The CARE-BMT score predicts cardiovascular events after hematopoietic cell transplantation but does not incorporate post-transplant cyclophosphamide (PTCy). We aimed to externally validate the original CARE-BMT score and a modified version incorporating standard-dose PTCy exposure in patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) undergoing allo-HCT.
Methods

We conducted a retrospective multicenter study including 809 adults with AML who underwent first allo-HCT across 11 Spanish transplant centers. The original and modified CARE-BMT scores were retrospectively applied. The primary endpoint was the cumulative incidence of post-transplant cardiac events, with relapse and death considered competing risks.
Results

Sixty patients developed a cardiac event, corresponding to a cumulative incidence of 6.9% (95% CI, 5.2-8.8). Cardiac events were associated with inferior 3-year overall survival (50.1% vs 62.5%; P = 0.001) and higher 3-year NRM (21.3% vs 6.2%; P = 0.001). Using the original CARE-BMT score, patients were classified as intermediate-risk (n = 246) or high-risk (n = 563), with no low-risk patients identified. Cardiac event incidence was higher in the high-risk group (8.6% vs 3.0%; HR, 2.89; P = 0.005). The modified CARE-BMT score classified patients as low-risk (n = 85), intermediate-risk (n = 558), or high-risk (n = 166), with progressively increasing cardiac event incidence (2.4%, 6.1%, and 11.8%, respectively; P = 0.011). High-risk patients had a significantly greater risk of cardiac events than low-risk patients (HR, 5.37; P = 0.024).
Conclusions

In this AML allo-HCT cohort, cardiac events occurred in approximately 7% of patients and were associated with worse survival and increased NRM. Incorporating standard-dose PTCy improved risk stratification, supporting inclusion of transplant-specific variables in cardiovascular risk prediction after allo-HCT.

papers.t: Achieved hemoglobin is not a dosing target in MDS
Genomic and clinical landscape of RAS mutations in acute myeloid leukemia
papers.c: In patients treated with non-intensive, venetoclax-based regimens, RAS mutations were associated with markedly inferior OS in patients with NPM1 (HR=2.98, p=0.007) or IDH1/2 mutations (HR=4.06, p<0.001). These data inform risk stratification and development of RAS-targeting strategies in AML.
ab: RAS mutations are recurrent in acute myeloid leukemia (AML); yet, their genomic and clinical landscape remain poorly characterized. We analyzed centralized molecular profiling data in 8,553 patients with newly diagnosed AML. Of these, 1,775 (21%) harbored RAS mutations: NRAS in 1,103 (13%), KRAS in 445 (5%), and both in 227 (3%). RAS mutations primarily clustered in P-loop hotspots (G12/G13, 70%), with NRAS showing higher Q61 mutation prevalence (24% vs. 9%) and KRAS showing additional K117/A146 hotspots. Multiple RAS mutations occurred in 23% of patients. Convergent evolution of RAS signaling mutations emerged as a key feature of RASmut AML. RTK/RAS pathway mutations were non-uniformly enriched: PTPN11, KIT and FLT3-TKD mutations were positively associated, CBL mutations showed no association, and FLT3-ITD mutations were negatively associated. The prognostic impact of RAS mutations was dependent on the genomic background and treatment. In multivariate analyses in intensively treated patients, NRAS mutations showed opposing associations with overall survival (OS): adverse in patients with AML, myelodysplasia-related (HR=1.32, p=0.036) and favorable in those with NPM1 (HR=0.61, p=0.036) or FLT3-ITD (HR=0.63, p=0.048) mutations, among others. KRAS mutations predicted inferior OS (HR=1.41; p=0.003). In patients treated with non-intensive, venetoclax-based regimens, RAS mutations were associated with markedly inferior OS in patients with NPM1 (HR=2.98, p=0.007) or IDH1/2 mutations (HR=4.06, p<0.001). These data inform risk stratification and development of RAS-targeting strategies in AML.

papers.t: SOHO State of the Art Updates and Next Questions | The Evolving AML Treatment Paradigm
papers.c: We explore growing evidence that guides the use of lower-intensity therapy in younger AML patients who would traditionally receive IC but may achieve favorable outcomes using HMA-Ven. When considering the use of HMA-Ven in younger patients, we highlight several important issues including the need for improved patient selection for HMA-Ven, optimal implementation of HMA-Ven in patients planned for allogeneic stem cell transplant (HCT), evaluation of post-HCT outcomes following induction using HMA-Ven, utilization of measurable residual disease (MRD) during treatment with HMA-Ven, and the prospect of triple combinations incorporating novel targeted agents.
ab: The treatment paradigm for fit, younger adults with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is evolving toward the frontline use of lower-intensity, better-tolerated therapies that more effectively target disease biology. For over 45 years, intensive chemotherapy (IC) has endured as the cornerstone of induction therapy for fit AML patients. Clinical outcomes have slowly improved during this time; however, long-term survival remains suboptimal, and IC-related toxicity is significant. For older AML patients, clinical outcomes have been transformed by the introduction of hypomethylating agents in combination with venetoclax (HMA-Ven) because of its potent anti-leukemic activity and improved tolerability. The success of HMA-Ven highlights the importance of rationally designed therapies that exploit leukemia dependencies while minimizing systemic toxicity. We outline the development of IC and HMA-Ven while also describing the first studies to directly compare these distinct modalities in younger patients. We explore growing evidence that guides the use of lower-intensity therapy in younger AML patients who would traditionally receive IC but may achieve favorable outcomes using HMA-Ven. When considering the use of HMA-Ven in younger patients, we highlight several important issues including the need for improved patient selection for HMA-Ven, optimal implementation of HMA-Ven in patients planned for allogeneic stem cell transplant (HCT), evaluation of post-HCT outcomes following induction using HMA-Ven, utilization of measurable residual disease (MRD) during treatment with HMA-Ven, and the prospect of triple combinations incorporating novel targeted agents.

papers.t: Perspectives on FDA Guidance for Myelodysplastic Syndromes
Oral azacitidine as time-limited, PCR-dependent maintenance in acute myeloid leukemia with inv(16): two case reports
papers.c: In case 2, a suicide attempt related to anticipated hospitalization precluded HiDAC; azacitidine was administered intermittently. Both patients remain MRD-negative 1.5 years post-treatment suggesting time-limited, MRD-guided azacitidine as a potential alternative to HiDAC consolidation.
ab: Core-binding factor acute myeloid leukemia (CBF-AML) in fit patients is treated with curative-intent induction chemotherapy followed by 3-4 cycles of high-dose cytarabine (HiDAC) consolidation. No standard therapy exists for patients with contraindications to HiDAC consolidation. Oral azacitidine is approved as indefinite maintenance therapy for intermediate/high risk AML but has not been studied in CBF-AML, nor in a time-limited fashion. We present two patients with CBF-AML who achieved morphologic remission after induction but had medical (case 1) or psychiatric (case 2) contraindications to HiDAC, therefore receiving oral azacitidine in a minimal residual disease (MRD)-guided, time-limited fashion. In case 1, drug-induced liver injury precluded HiDAC therapy; after four cycles, CBFB::MYH11 became PCR-undetectable, and azacitidine continued for a year. In case 2, a suicide attempt related to anticipated hospitalization precluded HiDAC; azacitidine was administered intermittently. Both patients remain MRD-negative 1.5 years post-treatment suggesting time-limited, MRD-guided azacitidine as a potential alternative to HiDAC consolidation.

papers.t: Optical genome mapping reveals a MYC-amplified ring chromosome arising through chromoanagenesis in AML
NFS1 as a Metabolic Vulnerability in Acute Myeloid Leukemia Through Iron Dysregulation and STAT1/IFIT2-Associated Signaling
papers.c: Furthermore, NFS1 knockdown enhanced the in vitro sensitivity of AML cells to azacitidine, venetoclax, and bortezomib. Collectively, this study suggests that NFS1 may represent a metabolic vulnerability in AML that links its depletion to iron dysregulation, apoptotic and ferroptosis-like cell death, and STAT1/IFIT2-associated signaling, providing a rationale for further investigation of NFS1 as a potential therapeutic target in AML.
ab: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a metabolically heterogeneous malignancy with poor outcomes and limited durable therapeutic options. We investigated NFS1, a key enzyme involved in iron-sulfur cluster biogenesis, as a potential metabolic vulnerability in AML. NFS1 was overexpressed in AML samples, and higher expression was associated with inferior overall survival in the TCGA-LAML cohort. Genetic knockdown of NFS1 markedly suppressed AML cell proliferation in vitro and reduced tumor growth in subcutaneous xenograft models. NFS1 knockdown induced disturbances in iron homeostasis accompanied by increased reactive oxygen species production and lipid peroxidation, together with reduced GPX4 expression. Together with the partial restoration of cell viability by ferrostatin-1, deferoxamine, and Z-VAD-FMK, these changes were consistent with concurrent apoptotic and ferroptosis-like cell death. Transcriptomic analysis revealed enrichment of type I interferon-related signaling pathways, while experimental validation demonstrated increased STAT1 phosphorylation at Tyr701 and increased expression of the downstream effector IFIT2. IFIT2 knockdown partially reversed the anti-proliferative effects of NFS1 knockdown, supporting an association between the growth-suppressive phenotype induced by NFS1 knockdown and STAT1/IFIT2-associated signaling. NFS1 knockdown was also accompanied by increased expression of PD-L1 and elevated concentrations of inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and IL-8, and reduced CD80 expression in THP-1-derived macrophage-like cells in an in vitro co-culture system. These findings indicate that NFS1 depletion is associated with immune-related transcriptional and phenotypic changes in vitro. Furthermore, NFS1 knockdown enhanced the in vitro sensitivity of AML cells to azacitidine, venetoclax, and bortezomib. Collectively, this study suggests that NFS1 may represent a metabolic vulnerability in AML that links its depletion to iron dysregulation, apoptotic and ferroptosis-like cell death, and STAT1/IFIT2-associated signaling, providing a rationale for further investigation of NFS1 as a potential therapeutic target in AML.

papers.t: Cord blood-derived natural killer cells engineered with a novel, highaffinity chimeric antigen receptor can eliminate acute myeloid leukemia cells with minimal C-type lectin-like molecule-1 expression
papers.c: Additionally, treatment with 2-23 CAR NK cells, but not M26 CAR NK cells, significantly enhanced the survival of the mice transplanted with CLL-1dim AML cells in vivo. Furthermore, in AML patient-derived xenograft models, the 2-23 CAR NK cells expanded robustly, persisted, and eradicated AML cells.
ab: CAR NK cell therapy is expected to be developed to treat acute myeloid leukemia (AML). C-type lectin-like molecule 1 (CLL-1) is a candidate target. However, AML cells with minimal CLL-1 expression (CLL-1dim) may not be eliminated by CAR NK cells. Here we demonstrate that cord blood (CB)-derived NK cells transduced with a novel high-affinity CAR that recognizes CLL-1 can eliminate CLL-1dim AML cells. A newly established anti- CLL-1 monoclonal antibody (mAb) designated as 2-23 exhibits a higher affinity for CLL- 1 than the widely used anti-CLL-1 mAb M26. CB-derived NK cells transduced with a CAR derived from 2-23, but not M26, killed CLL-1dim AML cells in vitro. Additionally, treatment with 2-23 CAR NK cells, but not M26 CAR NK cells, significantly enhanced the survival of the mice transplanted with CLL-1dim AML cells in vivo. Furthermore, in AML patient-derived xenograft models, the 2-23 CAR NK cells expanded robustly, persisted, and eradicated AML cells.

papers.t: A stem cell-based flow cytometry assay to predict post-transplantation relapse in patients with myelodysplastic syndromes with excess blasts: a prospective study
papers.c: Our data suggest the potential superiority of the PD MDS-SC-based assay over the traditional MFC method for outcome prediction in MDS-EB patients.
ab: Background

We aim to investigate whether the myelodysplastic syndrome stem cell (MDS-SC)-based assay could be used to predict relapse and survival after treatment in patients with MDS with excess blasts (MDS-EB).
Methods

A total of 143 cases receiving allografting were prospectively enrolled. A single-cell proteogenomic technique was used to evaluate the characteristics of CD34+ MDS subsets. These cells were detected using multiparameter flow cytometry (MFC) at diagnosis and post-treatment.
Results

The phenotypically defined (PD) CD34+CD38-cocktail+ (CD56/CD22/CD11b/CD7/Tim-3/CLL-1) MDS-SCs exhibited greater stemness and quiescence than PD CD34+CD38-MDS-SCs with other immunophenotypes. A high level of pre-transplantation PD CD34+CD38-cocktail+MDS-SCs (≥0.1064%) independently predicted 3-year cumulative incidence of relapse (CIR, P<0.001). No association of pre-transplantation traditional MFC-based MDS cells with relapse was observed. Patients with positive post-transplantation PD CD34+CD38-cocktail+MDS-SCs (≥0.0081%) experienced a higher 3-year CIR (40.4% vs. 6.5%, P<0.001) and lower disease-free survival (DFS, 57.4% vs. 85.1%, P<0.001) than those negative cases. Multivariate analysis revealed that positive post-transplantation PD CD34+CD38-cocktail+MDS-SCs independently predicted CIR (P<0.001) and DFS (P<0.001). Patients with post-transplantation traditional MFC-MRD positivity also had a higher CIR (60.0% vs. 12.8%, P<0.001) and lower DFS (40.0% vs. 80.2%, P<0.001) than those negative cases. The MDS-SC-based assay has higher sensitivity and C-index for MRD detection than the traditional MFC method.
Conclusion
Our data suggest the potential superiority of the PD MDS-SC-based assay over the traditional MFC method for outcome prediction in MDS-EB patients.

papers.t: Immune and cellular determinants of response to HMA-venetoclax regimens in acute myeloid leukemia
papers.c: Resistant AMLs showed stem-like dedifferentiation and sustained EMT. LAG-3 expression marked dysfunctional T cell states and emerged as a potential biomarker and therapeutic target.
ab: Hypomethylating agents (HMAs) combined with Venetoclax have reshaped the therapeutic landscape of acute myeloid leukemia (AML), yet the biological determinants of response remain unclear. We integrated clinical and genomic profiling in 132 newly diagnosed or relapsed/refractory AML patients treated with HMA-Venetoclax and performed single-cell RNA sequencing and T cell receptor (TCR) profiling in 10 newly diagnosed cases to define cellular and immune correlates of response. Response rates and survival aligned with published data. DNA Sequencing confirmed the favorable impact of IDH2 and the poor prognosis of TP53 mutations. scRNA-seq and TCR analysis showed that responders exhibited expansion of cytotoxic CD8+ T cells, increased TCR clonal diversity, and activation of antigen-presentation pathways. Nonresponders displayed baseline inflammatory signaling, impaired myeloid maturation, and a suppressive microenvironment enriched in IDO1+ dendritic cells. Resistant AMLs showed stem-like dedifferentiation and sustained EMT. LAG-3 expression marked dysfunctional T cell states and emerged as a potential biomarker and therapeutic target.

papers.t: Rapid molecular screening of adult AML: Experience from the Spanish CETLAM cooperative group
papers.c: However, 74% of patients initially classified as intermediate-risk were reclassified as adverse-risk upon integration of NGS and cytogenetics. This CETLAM initiative demonstrates that a centralized molecular platform is a feasible and reliable strategy for early risk stratification and therapeutic decision-making in AML within a multicentre setting.
ab: Genetic testing is essential for risk stratification and early therapeutic decision-making in acute myeloid leukaemia (AML). While 2022 European LeukemiaNet (ELN) guidelines recommend a 3-5-day turnaround time for key molecular markers, next-generation sequencing (NGS) often extends to 15 days in clinical practice. In this study, we evaluated the first-year results of a centralized rapid screening platform for 15 hospitals in the Grupo Cooperativo de Estudio y Tratamiento de las Leucemias Agudas y Mielodisplasias (CETLAM) cooperative group, modelled after the German-Austrian Acute Myeloid Leukaemia Study Group (AMLSG) diagnostic strategy. We prospectively enrolled 211 consecutive adult patients with de novo AML. A centralized laboratory performed nucleic acid purification, biobanking and high-priority molecular analysis including nucleophosmin 1 (NPM1), Fms-like tyrosine kinase 3 (FLT3-ITD/TKD), CCAAT enhancer binding protein alpha (CEBPA), isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 and 2 (IDH1/2), lysine methyltransferase 2A (KMT2A-PTD), upstream binding transcription factor (UBTF-TD) and 10 key fusions using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and capillary electrophoresis. Results were compared with local NGS and cytogenetics to assess diagnostic accuracy and ELN risk reclassification. The mean analytical turnaround time was 3-4 days for high-priority mutations and 7 days for gene fusions. Initial rapid screening accurately identified 98% of favourable-risk cases. However, 74% of patients initially classified as intermediate-risk were reclassified as adverse-risk upon integration of NGS and cytogenetics. This CETLAM initiative demonstrates that a centralized molecular platform is a feasible and reliable strategy for early risk stratification and therapeutic decision-making in AML within a multicentre setting.

papers.t: Inhibition of PHB2/PINK1-mediated mitophagy potentiates venetoclax activity in acute myeloid leukemia
papers.c: Notably, both genetic depletion of PINK1 or PHB2, as well as pharmacological inhibition of PHB2, significantly increased AML cell sensitivity to venetoclax both in vitro and in vivo. Together, these findings highlight the potential of targeting the PHB2/PINK1 signalling pathway to improve the efficacy of venetoclax-based therapies in AML by disrupting the mitophagy process.
ab: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cells are highly dependent on mitochondrial activity for survival, with this metabolic reliance driven in part by BCL-2, which is therapeutically targeted by venetoclax-based therapies. The regulation of mitochondrial dynamics in leukemic cells is therefore essential for maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis. However, the mechanisms that enable selective degradation of damaged mitochondria (mitophagy) are still poorly understood in AML. In this study, we sought to elucidate the role of PTEN-induced putative kinase 1 (PINK1), a key sensor of mitochondrial stress, in regulating mitophagy in leukemic cells. Our results identified PINK1 as a central modulator of mitophagy. Genetic depletion of PINK1 reduced both basal and stress-induced mitophagy, leading to mitochondria accumulation and functional impairment. Additionally, we discovered that PINK1 stabilization during mitochondrial stress is regulated by Prohibitin 2 (PHB2), and that depletion or inhibition of PHB2 mirrored the biological effects of PINK1 loss. Notably, both genetic depletion of PINK1 or PHB2, as well as pharmacological inhibition of PHB2, significantly increased AML cell sensitivity to venetoclax both in vitro and in vivo. Together, these findings highlight the potential of targeting the PHB2/PINK1 signalling pathway to improve the efficacy of venetoclax-based therapies in AML by disrupting the mitophagy process.

papers.t: Germline DDX41 defines a distinct subgroup in MDS undergoing transplantation with reduced relapse and improved survival
papers.c: Adjusted models showed significantly improved disease-free survival (DFS) for P/LP DDX41 (hazard ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.41-0.95; p=0.03) and no significant association with non-relapse mortality (NRM) or graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). In summary, these findings identify DDX41-associated MDS as a transplant subgroup with superior DFS regardless of conditioning intensity driven by reduced relapse risk and lack of excess NRM and GVHD supporting incorporation of germline DDX41 status into transplant planning.
ab: Germline DDX41 variants are a recognized cause of adult myelodysplastic neoplasms (MDS), characterized by distinct biological features and favorable prognosis. The independent effect of DDX41 status on outcomes after allogeneic transplantation, the role of conditioning intensity, and treatment-related toxicity risk remain unresolved. To address this gap, we analyzed 1,514 patients with MDS undergoing transplantation prior to routine DDX41 testing alongside a wild-type comparator, providing an unbiased benchmark for this molecular subgroup. Forty-nine patients (3.2%) carried pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP) germline DDX41 variants; 19 (39%) had an additional somatic DDX41 mutation, most commonly p.R525H. P/LP DDX41 cases were older (median 63 vs 59 years) and showed lower IPSS-M risk with absent TP53 mutations (0% vs 21%). In terms of outcome, 2-year relapse incidence was significantly lower in P/LP DDX41 (17% vs 34%, p=0.01). In multivariable analysis, the presence of a DDX41 P/LP variant independently associated with lower risk of relapse (hazard ratio 0.43, 95% CI 0.21-0.88; p=0.02), concentrated in the reduced-intensity/nonmyeloablative stratum. Adjusted models showed significantly improved disease-free survival (DFS) for P/LP DDX41 (hazard ratio 0.62, 95% CI 0.41-0.95; p=0.03) and no significant association with non-relapse mortality (NRM) or graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). In summary, these findings identify DDX41-associated MDS as a transplant subgroup with superior DFS regardless of conditioning intensity driven by reduced relapse risk and lack of excess NRM and GVHD supporting incorporation of germline DDX41 status into transplant planning.

papers.t: Real-World Survival Outcomes of Venetoclax Combination Therapies in Acute Myeloid Leukemia: Impact of Minimal Residual Disease Status and Antifungal Prophylaxis
papers.c: We conclude that AML patients in remission with venetoclax combinations may still be consolidated, and potentially cured, by HSCT, even after failure of intensive chemotherapy. Posaconazole prophylaxis effectively reduces risk of severe fungal infections, but a concomitant venetoclax dose of 50 mg may be sub-optimal.
ab: In recent years the addition of the oral BCL2 inhibitor venetoclax to hypomethylating agents (HMAs) has emerged as the standard-of-care for patients with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) who are not fit for intensive chemotherapy, significantly improving survival and quality-of-life. Venetoclax is metabolized mainly by cytochrome P450 3A4 enzymes and serves as a P-glycoprotein substrate, which make it largely affected by interactions with drugs. Dose reductions are needed to allow mold active antifungal prophylaxis, but there is no consensus on the exact venetoclax target dose concomitantly with posaconazole. We report on efficacy and safety of venetoclax combinations in 38 first-line (FL) and 51 relapsed-refractory (R/R) AML patients. Although complete remission (CR) rate was lower in R/R than in FL (49% vs. 68%; p = 0.08), achievement of this status was associated with comparable median overall survival (OS) in R/R and FL (13.67 vs. 13.72 months). Eighteen (20%) patients underwent allogenic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) with a 2-year OS probability of 66.7%. Although antifungal prophylaxis was associated with a lower rate of grade 3-4 fungal infections (6% vs. 24%, p 0.044), patients treated with venetoclax daily dose of 50 mg with posaconazole had significantly shorter mOS in multivariate analysis (16.5 vs. 4.5 months; p 0.011). We conclude that AML patients in remission with venetoclax combinations may still be consolidated, and potentially cured, by HSCT, even after failure of intensive chemotherapy. Posaconazole prophylaxis effectively reduces risk of severe fungal infections, but a concomitant venetoclax dose of 50 mg may be sub-optimal.

papers.t: Interpreting the Association Between Plasma Citrulline and Bloodstream Infection in Pediatric Acute Myeloid Leukemia
Apoptosis gene expression analysis identifies biologically distinct AML clusters and BIK as an independent prognostic marker
papers.c: Analysis of individual genes showed that higher BIK mRNA expression was associated with poorer survival and lack of response to VenAza, highlighting the paradoxical association between increased expression of this pro-apoptotic gene and adverse clinical outcome. These findings demonstrate that dysregulation of apoptosis-related gene expression defines clinically distinct AML subgroups and may contribute to differences in prognosis and therapeutic response.
ab: Dysregulation of apoptosis is a key feature of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and contributes to therapy resistance, yet the clinical relevance of apoptosis-related gene expression remains incompletely understood. We prospectively analyzed mRNA expression of apoptosis-related genes in bone marrow mononuclear cells from 90 newly diagnosed AML patients. Gene expression clustering identified two biologically distinct patient groups. The subgroup with significantly inferior overall survival (Cluster 2) showed coordinated upregulation of pro-apoptotic genes, including BCL2L11 (BIM), BBC3 (PUMA), BID, BAD, BIK, and BAX, together with a shift in anti-apoptotic signaling toward lower BCL2 expression and increased expression of alternative survival regulators, MCL1 and BCL2L1 (BCL-xL). Reduced expression of executioner caspases CASP3 and CASP7 was also observed in Cluster 2, which may indicate less efficient apoptotic execution. Among patients treated with venetoclax + azacitidine (VenAza), Cluster 2 demonstrated significantly shorter event-free survival. This finding is consistent with the biological features of Cluster 2, including a monocytic immunophenotype previously associated with reduced sensitivity to BCL-2-targeted therapy and increased reliance on alternative anti-apoptotic regulators such as MCL1 and BCL-xL. Analysis of individual genes showed that higher BIK mRNA expression was associated with poorer survival and lack of response to VenAza, highlighting the paradoxical association between increased expression of this pro-apoptotic gene and adverse clinical outcome. These findings demonstrate that dysregulation of apoptosis-related gene expression defines clinically distinct AML subgroups and may contribute to differences in prognosis and therapeutic response.

papers.t: Chimeric Antigen Receptor T-Cell Therapy in T Cell/Histiocyte-Rich Large B-Cell Lymphoma: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
papers.c: Low- and high-grade cytokine release syndrome occurred in 68.3% and 4.5% of patients while low- and high-grade immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome was seen in 23.1% and 12.9% of the patients. Overall, no unexpected safety signals were identified in r/r THRLBCL patients receiving CAR T-cell therapy but durable responses were only achieved in a subset of patients.
ab: T-cell/histiocyte-rich large B-cell lymphoma (THRLBCL) is a rare subtype of B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma with an aggressive clinical course and poor prognosis in the case of relapsed or refractory (r/r) disease. Recently, anti-CD19 chimeric antigen-receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has been approved for the treatment of large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL), but subgroup-specific outcomes in these patients have never been reported. Therefore, only limited retrospective data on the safety and efficacy of CAR T-cell therapy in r/r THRLBCL is available. To comprehensively evaluate outcomes of CAR T-cell recipients with r/r THRLBCL, we performed a systematic literature review (SLR) and meta-analysis (MA). The SLR identified seven studies including 157 patients with r/r THRLBCL. Pooled overall response rates and complete remission rates were 48.3% and 30.4%, respectively. Median progression-free survival was 3.4 months, with a 12-month rate of 29.1% and median overall survival was 15.0 months, with a 12-month rate of 57.4%. Low- and high-grade cytokine release syndrome occurred in 68.3% and 4.5% of patients while low- and high-grade immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome was seen in 23.1% and 12.9% of the patients. Overall, no unexpected safety signals were identified in r/r THRLBCL patients receiving CAR T-cell therapy but durable responses were only achieved in a subset of patients.

papers.t: Outcomes of Allogeneic Stem Cell Transplantation in a North American Adult T Cell Leukemia/Lymphoma Cohort
papers.c: This is the largest cohort evaluating HCT outcomes in a NA-ATLL population. Alternative donor HCT may expand access to HCT without an apparent increase in non-relapse mortality in this selected cohort. Clinical acute disease subtype shows inferior outcomes compared to lymphomatous subtype. Baseline performance status is a predictor of improved prognosis post-transplant. These data suggest that fit patients should proceed to HCT expeditiously with any donor option available.
ab: Background

Adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL) is an and aggressive mature T-cell neoplasm driven by human T-cell leukemia virus type 1 (HTLV-1) with dismal prognosis. North American ATLL (NA-ATLL) disproportionately impacts individuals of Afro-Caribbean and Latin American descent who face significant disparities in identifying conventional 8/8 HLA-matched donors in international registries. While allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT) is established in East Asian cohorts, outcomes data in Western populations remain limited. We aimed to evaluate post-HCT survival, toxicities, and prognostic risk factors in NA-ATLL.
Objective

The objective of this study was to evaluate HCT clinical outcomes. Our primary outcome was overall survival (OS), and secondary outcomes included progression-free survival (PFS), non-relapse mortality (NRM), and graft-versus-host disease (GVHD). We tested the hypotheses that alternative donor HCT yields comparable survival to matched donor HCT and assessed variables that may dictate post-transplant survival.
Study Design

This was a multicenter retrospective registry study evaluating 46 adult patients with NA-ATLL who underwent allogeneic HCT across participating North American centers. Myeloablative conditioning regimens were myeloablative in 21.7%, and alternative donor HCT (without a matched donor) were used in 54.3%. Survival endpoints (OS, PFS) were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method and compared via log-rank tests. Cumulative incidences of relapse, NRM, acute GVHD, and chronic GVHD were calculated considering competing risks. Independent prognostic variables were evaluated using Cox multivariable proportional hazards regression analysis.
Results

There was no significant difference in OS or PFS between those who received matched versus alternative donor HCT (OS p = 0.601, PFS p = 0.376). Patients with acute disease subtype had worse OS compared to lymphomatous (logrank p = 0.043, 3-year OS 22.2% versus 52.3%, respectively). Acute GVHD yielded a 1-year cumulative incidence rate of 45.7% (95%CI; 30.7-59.5%) while that of chronic GVHD was 18.5% (95%CI; 8.5-31.5%). Twenty-seven patients were deceased at time of analysis, primarily due to relapse-related causes in 17 patients. In multivariable analysis, lymphomatous disease subtype (HR 0.3, 95%CI 0.1-0.88, p = 0.027) and Karnofsky performance score of ≥80 (HR 0.26, 95%CI 0.09-0.73, p = 0.01) were significant predictors of OS.
Conclusion

This is the largest cohort evaluating HCT outcomes in a NA-ATLL population. Alternative donor HCT may expand access to HCT without an apparent increase in non-relapse mortality in this selected cohort. Clinical acute disease subtype shows inferior outcomes compared to lymphomatous subtype. Baseline performance status is a predictor of improved prognosis post-transplant. These data suggest that fit patients should proceed to HCT expeditiously with any donor option available.

papers.t: EZH2 mutation status predicts inferior outcomes after bendamustine-based immunochemotherapy in frontline follicular lymphoma: A GELTAMO multicenter validation study
Zanubrutinib monotherapy in CD79B-mutated relapsed or refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma: A multicenter Phase 2 study
Real-World Treatment Patterns, Burden of Illness, and Survival of Autologous Stem Cell Transplant-Ineligible Patients With Mantle Cell Lymphoma in Ontario, Canada
papers.c: This study characterized the treatment patterns, rwOS, and TTNT-D of MCL patients in Ontario, Canada. Poor real-world clinical outcomes support the need for additional 1L and R/R therapies for MCL management for an ASCT-ineligible population.
ab: Introduction

Since the approval of ibrutinib in 2016 in Canada for relapsed or refractory (R/R) mantle cell lymphoma (MCL), there has been limited evidence characterizing treatment patterns, burden of illness, and survival in Canadian patients ineligible for autologous stem cell transplant (ASCT). This is the first study in Ontario reporting real-world treatment patterns and clinical outcomes of elderly patients with MCL who are transplant-ineligible in 1L and R/R settings.
Methods

The aim of this study was to characterize the real-world use and outcomes of patients with MCL who were ≥ 65 years old and transplant-ineligible in first-line (1L) and R/R settings between 2013 and 2021 using administrative databases in Ontario, Canada. Incidence of MCL, treatment patterns, and overall survival (OS) were assessed.
Results

The study cohort consisted of 754 patients (follow-up: 36.1 months, median age: 76 [IQR: 71-82], 71.1% male). Most patients received bendamustine and rituximab in 1L (76.7%) and ibrutinib in second-line (2L; 73.2%). Mortality rates following 1L and 2L therapy were 39.3% and 68.5%, respectively. Duration of therapy in 1L and 2L treatment was 4.70 and 2.14 months, respectively. Median OS decreased with subsequent lines of therapy (1L: 3.51 years; 2L: 0.60 years; third-line: 0.43 years).
Conclusion

This study characterized the treatment patterns, rwOS, and TTNT-D of MCL patients in Ontario, Canada. Poor real-world clinical outcomes support the need for additional 1L and R/R therapies for MCL management for an ASCT-ineligible population.
Trial Registration
The authors have confirmed clinical trial registration is not needed for this submission.

papers.t: Allogeneic versus autologous stem cell transplantation for extranodal NK/T-Cell lymphoma: A systematic review and meta-analysis
The Use of Bruton-Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors in Non-IgM Lymphoplasmacytic Lymphoma: A Retrospective Italian Study
Ablation of CDK6 and STAT5B rewires T cell developmental dynamics and prevents ALK+ lymphoma formation
papers.c: A transcriptional signature derived from CDK6/STAT5B-dependent tumor initiation genes identifies a high-risk subgroup of ALCL patients with worse survival. Together, these findings establish a molecular link between thymocyte development, the crosstalk of CDK6 and STAT5B, oncogenic signaling, and clinical outcome in ALCL.
ab: CDK6 and STAT5B are well-established oncogenic drivers, but their interplay during transformation remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that simultaneous genetic deletion of Cdk6 and Stat5b in an NPM-ALKTg/+ mouse model completely prevents tumor formation. Immature DN2/3 thymocytes are identified as the cellular origin of ALK-driven malignancy. Single-cell transcriptomics reveals a tumor-specific differentiation trajectory that is fully disrupted by combined Cdk6/Stat5b loss, coinciding with a developmental shift. We uncover shared transcriptional targets of CDK6 and STAT5B involved in cell-cycle regulation and apoptosis at the tumor initiation stage. In human ALCL cells, dual deletion of CDK6 and STAT5B induces context-dependent synthetic lethality, exposing a potential therapeutic vulnerability. A transcriptional signature derived from CDK6/STAT5B-dependent tumor initiation genes identifies a high-risk subgroup of ALCL patients with worse survival. Together, these findings establish a molecular link between thymocyte development, the crosstalk of CDK6 and STAT5B, oncogenic signaling, and clinical outcome in ALCL.

papers.t: Comorbidity Burden and Prognosis in Patients Aged 80+ Years With Large B-Cell Lymphoma
papers.c: Multimorbidity strongly predicts outcomes in LBCL patients aged 80+ years. The simplified MaSH-CI adds prognostic value beyond conventional prognostic indices and offers a practical tool for risk-adapted management.
ab: Background

Patients aged 80+ years with large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL) represent a growing, vulnerable population where conventional prognostic indices inadequately capture comorbidity burden. We evaluated prognostic value of the Lymphoma Epidemiology of Outcomes Comorbidity Index (LCI) and derived simplified comorbidity model.
Methods

In 539 patients aged 80+ years with LBCL from two independent international cohorts, we evaluated associations between comorbidities/LCI (10 comorbidity categories) and overall survival (OS) or event-free survival (EFS). discrimination and model fit were assessed using C-indices and likelihood ratio tests.
Results

LCI categories were 0 (19%), 1 (31%), 2+ (50%). Higher LCI predicted inferior OS (LCI 1 vs. 0: hazard ratio [HR] = 1.43 [95% CI 1.04-1.97]; LCI 2+ vs. 0: HR = 1.88 [1.40-2.53]), EFS (LCI 1 vs. 0: HR = 1.37 [1.00-1.87]; LCI 2+ vs. 0: HR = 1.78 [1.33-2.38]), and higher 2-year nonlymphoma mortality (11%, 13%, and 26% for LCI 0, 1, and 2+). Heart disease (48%), prior or concurrent malignancy (9%), and stroke (8%) independently predicted OS and were combined into the MaSH Comorbidity Index (MaSH-CI; one point each), with scores 0 (44%), 1 (47%), and 2+ (9%). Higher MaSH-CI predicted inferior OS (1 vs. 0: HR = 1.59 [1.27-1.98]; 2+ vs. 0: HR = 2.43 [1.70-3.47]). Adding LCI or MaSH-CI to International Prognostic Index (IPI) or SENIOR-IPI significantly improved model fit and discrimination across all endpoints (ΔC-index 0.02-0.03).
Conclusion

Multimorbidity strongly predicts outcomes in LBCL patients aged 80+ years. The simplified MaSH-CI adds prognostic value beyond conventional prognostic indices and offers a practical tool for risk-adapted management.

papers.t: Reduced-dose pegylated asparaginase reliably achieves therapeutic levels in adult patients with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and lymphoblastic lymphoma
Loncastuximab and Rituximab in Elderly Unfit/Frail Patients With Previously Untreated Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma
papers.c: Additional investigation of targeted therapies in vulnerable unfit and frail patients with DLBCL is warranted. (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05144009).
ab: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) therapy is typically treated with multi-agent chemotherapy with curative intent but is often challenging or poorly tolerated in patients who are elderly, frail, or have significant comorbidities. LOTIS-9 was a phase 2 trial of loncastuximab tesirine (loncastuximab tesirine-lpyl [Lonca]) plus rituximab (Lonca-R) in patients with newly diagnosed DLBCL who were unfit (cohort A) or frail with or without cardiac comorbidities (cohort B), the majority of whom typically would be ineligible for trials. Patients received Lonca (150 µg/kg during cycles 1-2, 75 µg/kg for subsequent cycles) and R (375 mg/m2) intravenously Q3W for 3-6 cycles, adapted based on response after cycle 3. The primary endpoint of cohort A was complete response (CR) rate; coprimary endpoints of cohort B were CR rate and proportion of patients who completed treatment per protocol. The median age was 84 years (range, 80-91) in cohort A (n=17) and 80 years (range, 67-92) in cohort B (n=24). The CR rates were 52.9% (A: 9/17) and 41.7% (B: 10/24), respectively. In cohort B, 8 (33.3%) patients completed treatment. Grade ≥3 adverse events occurred in 31 (75.6%) patients, including 11 fatal events. Due to toxicity concerns in this medically fragile population, LOTIS-9 was voluntarily terminated prematurely though meaningful efficacy was demonstrated in patients who typically would be ineligible for clinical trials and/or standard of care therapies. These findings provide important insights for future trials. Additional investigation of targeted therapies in vulnerable unfit and frail patients with DLBCL is warranted. (ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05144009).

papers.t: A Myeloma Masquerade: CCND3-Rearranged Plasma Cell Myeloma Mimicking Lymphoplasmacytic Lymphoma
Long-term mental health service utilization among patients with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma: a population-based study
papers.c: Higher MHU was associated with younger age, female sex, lower income, and urban residence. DLBCL patients demonstrated persistently elevated MHU for up to 15 years post-treatment, underscoring the need for mental health integration into survivorship care.
ab: Mental health disorders are common in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), yet long-term mental health service utilization (MHU) remains poorly characterized. We evaluated MHU rates and associated sociodemographic factors in patients undergoing curative treatment. This population-based retrospective matched-cohort study used Ontario administrative data; patients treated with rituximab-based chemotherapy (2005-2017) were matched 1:4 (age/sex) to non-cancer controls and followed up to 15 years. Difference-in-differences Poisson regression compared MHU between groups, adjusting for sociodemographic variables. Among 10,132 patients and 40,528 controls, DLBCL patients had significantly higher adjusted MHU at 5 years: outpatient visits (aRR 1.22), emergency visits (aRR 1.75), and hospitalizations (aRR 1.97). Elevated rates persisted at 10 and 15 years. Higher MHU was associated with younger age, female sex, lower income, and urban residence. DLBCL patients demonstrated persistently elevated MHU for up to 15 years post-treatment, underscoring the need for mental health integration into survivorship care.

papers.t: Improving survival and narrowing age disparities in mantle cell lymphoma across therapeutic eras
Impact of Prophylactic Steroids on CAR T-cell Related Toxicity for Relapsed and Refractory Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma
papers.c: Prophylactic corticosteroids did not impact CRS, ICANS, response rates, or survival. Although CRS onset may be modestly delayed, these findings do not support routine steroid prophylaxis in CAR-T-treated NHL patients.
ab: Background

Anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy (CAR-T) has transformed the treatment of relapsed/refractory (R/R) non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL). However, toxicities including cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) remain significant. Prophylactic corticosteroid use increased after cohort 6 of ZUMA-1, which suggested reduced severe CRS and ICANS, although the lack of a comparator arm limits interpretation.
Objective
To evaluate the impact of steroid prophylaxis on outcomes and toxicities in a real-world setting.
Study Design

We conducted a retrospective, single-institution analysis of adults (≥18 years) with R/R NHL treated with CD28 costimulated axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel) or brexucabtagene autoleucel (brexu-cel) at The Ohio State University (2018-2023). All patients received steroid prophylaxis (dexamethasone 10 mg daily × 3 from infusion day). Outcomes including toxicities (CRS, ICANS) and response rates, survival outcomes, and hazard ratios were compared using logistic regression, log-rank test, and Cox model.
Results

137 patients received CAR-T (axi-cel n=118, brexu-cel n=19); 27.0% received steroid prophylaxis (PPX). Baseline characteristics were similar between groups, although primary refractory disease differed. CRS and ICANS prevalence did not significantly differ between cohorts. Any-grade CRS occurred in 97.3% of patients with PPX vs 88.0% with no PPX (p=0.13), with grade 3-4 CRS in 2.7% vs 12.0% (p=0.13). ICANS occurred in 75.7% vs 68.0% (p=0.38), with grade 3-4 ICANS in 24.3% vs 32.0% (p=0.38). Median time to CRS onset was delayed in the PPX group (4 vs 3 days, p<0.01), with no difference in ICANS onset. Overall response rates (ORR) were 75.7% vs 69.0% (p=0.44); complete response rates (CRR) were 62.2% vs 54.0% (p=0.39). OS and PFS did not differ.
Conclusion

Prophylactic corticosteroids did not impact CRS, ICANS, response rates, or survival. Although CRS onset may be modestly delayed, these findings do not support routine steroid prophylaxis in CAR-T-treated NHL patients.

papers.t: Final analysis results from DREAMM-3, a phase 3 study of belantamab mafodotin versus pomalidomide plus dexamethasone in patients with relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma
IFM 2026 Recommendations for First-line Treatment of Newly Diagnosed Multiple Myeloma
papers.c: We discuss the role of measurable residual disease and NGS-based high-risk myeloma definition across both populations, and position these recommendations relative to the 2025 EHA-EMN evidence-based guidelines. Finally, we summarize ongoing trials investigating T-cell-redirecting immunotherapies (CAR-T cells and bispecific antibodies) as replacements for, or additions to, ASCT and maintenance therapy, which may further reshape the first-line treatment paradigm in the coming years.
ab: The treatment landscape of newly diagnosed multiple myeloma (NDMM) has changed considerably over the past 5 years. Anti-CD38-VRd quadruplets are now the standard of care for transplant-eligible patients and an important option for transplant-ineligible patients. This review presents unified, evidence-based first-line treatment recommendations from the Intergroupe Francophone du Myélome (IFM), covering transplant-eligible and transplant-ineligible NDMM within a single framework and common methodology. In transplant-eligible patients, daratumumab-VRd and isatuximab-VRd, informed respectively by the PERSEUS and GMMG-HD7 trials, are now the reference induction regimens, followed by autologous stem cell transplantation, optional consolidation, and daratumumab-lenalidomide maintenance. In transplant-ineligible patients, daratumumab-lenalidomide-dexamethasone (DRd), informed by the MAIA trial, remains the treatment backbone: in fit patients, adding bortezomib (isatuximab-VRd or daratumumab-VRd, informed by IMROZ, CEPHEUS, and BENEFIT) could further improve outcomes, while frail patients receive the same backbone without dexamethasone (DR), informed by IFM2017-03. Mathematical modeling projects a median progression-free survival of approximately 205 months with daratumumab-VRd in transplant-eligible patients (PERSEUS model) and approximately 100 months in transplant-ineligible/transplant-deferred patients (CEPHEUS model), approaching for the first time a normal life expectancy for a substantial subset of patients and supporting the emerging concept of functional cure. We discuss the role of measurable residual disease and NGS-based high-risk myeloma definition across both populations, and position these recommendations relative to the 2025 EHA-EMN evidence-based guidelines. Finally, we summarize ongoing trials investigating T-cell-redirecting immunotherapies (CAR-T cells and bispecific antibodies) as replacements for, or additions to, ASCT and maintenance therapy, which may further reshape the first-line treatment paradigm in the coming years.

papers.t: Frailty and quality of life in a real-world multiple myeloma population
papers.c: Frail RRMM patients reported unchanged global QoL and fatigue, and deterioration in physical functioning and more pain during follow-up. Our results based on a real-world population show that QoL findings from clinical trial populations cannot directly be applied to frail patients.
ab: Frailty is common in multiple myeloma (MM) and is associated with inferior outcomes. Knowledge on quality of life (QoL) primarily originates from clinical trials, where frail patients are often not included. In this nationwide, longitudinal observational study, QoL was assessed in 681 Danish patients with newly diagnosed MM (NDMM) or relapsed or refractory MM (RRMM) with symptomatic disease using patient-reported outcomes collected over 2 years of follow-up between 2017 and 2021. Patients were categorized as fit, intermediate-fit or frail according to the International Myeloma Working Group (IMWG) frailty score. Preselected QoL domains from the European Organization for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC) Quality of Life Core 30 (QLQ-C30), the Chemotherapy-Induced Peripheral Neuropathy module (EORTC QLQ-CIPN20) and the Short-form health survey (SF12) questionnaires were analysed using linear mixed models and interpreted in terms of clinical relevance. At inclusion, frail patients reported clinically relevant lower global QoL and physical functioning, and more fatigue compared to fit patients. Frail NDMM patients reported improvement in global QoL and pain during follow-up, whereas physical functioning and fatigue remained unchanged. Frail RRMM patients reported unchanged global QoL and fatigue, and deterioration in physical functioning and more pain during follow-up. Our results based on a real-world population show that QoL findings from clinical trial populations cannot directly be applied to frail patients.

papers.t: A Myeloma Masquerade: CCND3-Rearranged Plasma Cell Myeloma Mimicking Lymphoplasmacytic Lymphoma
Elevated Risks for Depression and Anxiety Following Diagnosis of Multiple Myeloma
papers.c: These findings demonstrate an elevated risk of depression and/or anxiety among patients with both symptomatic and smoldering MM and highlight the need for increased awareness of psychological morbidity, particularly during the first year after diagnosis.
ab: Background

Patients with multiple myeloma (MM) may be particularly vulnerable to depression and anxiety following diagnosis due to high disease burden, treatment-related side effects, and the incurable nature of the disease.
Methods

In this nationwide population-based cohort study, we used Danish population-based registries to investigate the risk of depression and anxiety in patients with MM (symptomatic MM and smoldering MM) compared with age- and sex-matched individuals from the general population.
Results

A total of 3861 patients with MM and 19 305 matched comparators were included (median age 73 years; 59% male). During follow-up, depression and/or anxiety occurred in 315 MM patients (8.2%) and 660 comparators (3.4%). MM was associated with a substantially increased risk of depression and/or anxiety (adjusted HR 2.56, 95% CI 2.23-2.94). The association was strongest among patients with symptomatic MM (adjusted HR 2.63, 95% CI 2.21-3.12) but remained elevated among patients with smoldering MM (adjusted HR 1.44, 95% CI 1.10-1.87). The association was strongest during the first year following diagnosis and attenuated over time.
Conclusion

These findings demonstrate an elevated risk of depression and/or anxiety among patients with both symptomatic and smoldering MM and highlight the need for increased awareness of psychological morbidity, particularly during the first year after diagnosis.

papers.t: Population Pharmacokinetic Estimation of Melphalan Exposure Predicts Disease Control and Toxicity after Autologous Hematopoietic Cell Transplantation for Multiple Myeloma
papers.c: Higher exposure by NCA and pop PK was also associated with day 100 measurable residual disease negativity (OR 0.47, 95% CI 0.23-0.96, P=0.038 and OR 0.40, 95% CI 0.19-0.81, P=0.011, respectively). These findings support prospective evaluation of pop PK-guided melphalan dosing to define an exposure range that optimizes efficacy while limiting toxicity.
ab: High-dose therapy (HDT) with melphalan followed by autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation (AHCT) remains standard for multiple myeloma (MM) consolidation. However, body surface area-based dosing results in interpatient variability in exposure, which may affect efficacy and toxicity. We retrospectively studied patients with MM who underwent AHCT and had serial melphalan concentrations measured after HDT. Melphalan area under the concentration-time curve (AUC) was calculated using non-compartmental analysis (NCA) and estimated using a two-compartment population pharmacokinetic (pop PK) model. 148 patients were included; median follow-up was 6.3 years. Median melphalan AUC was 12.7 mg*h/L by NCA and 14.0 mg*h/L by pop PK, with significant correlation between methods (r=0.64, P<0.001). Patients with NCA AUC equal to or above the median had superior 12- and 24-month progression-free survival compared with those below the median (75% vs 62% and 60% vs 44%, P=0.019). Pop PK AUC showed a similar trend (76% vs 61% and 57% vs 47%, P=0.11). Overall survival and non-relapse mortality did not differ by exposure. Higher exposure was associated with longer hospitalization, neutropenic fever days and more CTCAE v5.0 grade ≥3 nonhematologic toxicities. Higher pop PK AUC was associated with overall response at day 100 (OR 2.94, 95% CI, 1.04-9.60, P=0.041). Higher exposure by NCA and pop PK was also associated with day 100 measurable residual disease negativity (OR 0.47, 95% CI 0.23-0.96, P=0.038 and OR 0.40, 95% CI 0.19-0.81, P=0.011, respectively). These findings support prospective evaluation of pop PK-guided melphalan dosing to define an exposure range that optimizes efficacy while limiting toxicity.

papers.t: Plasma Exchange and Daratumumab for Myeloma Cast Nephropathy
papers.c: Daratumumab was not associated with kidney recovery at 90 days (OR 1.46, 95% CI: 0.84-2.55). Thus, in this multicenter cohort study, neither PLEX nor daratumumab was associated with kidney recovery at 90 days.
ab: Multiple myeloma light chain cast nephropathy (LCCN) is often treated with plasma exchange (PLEX) or the anti-CD38 monoclonal antibody, daratumumab. However, rigorous studies supporting these therapies for LCCN are limited. Using data from 25 U.S.-based academic cancer centers, we conducted two target trials examining the association between early receipt of PLEX or early receipt of daratumumab and kidney recovery in patients with newly diagnosed LCCN. Kidney recovery was defined as being alive, not on kidney replacement therapy, and with an improvement of at least one stage of AKI severity, all assessed at 90 days. Secondary outcomes included kidney recovery at 60 and 180 days. Logistic regression with propensity score overlap weights was used to adjust for confounders. Of 549 eligible patients for the PLEX target trial, 158 (28.8%) received PLEX. There was no association between PLEX and kidney recovery at 90 days (OR 1.48, 95% CI: 0.96-2.30). However, in subgroup analyses, PLEX was associated with higher odds of kidney recovery at 90 days among patients with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma compared to those with relapsed disease, as well as higher odds of kidney recovery among those with Stage 3 versus Stage 1 or 2 AKI at the time of LCCN diagnosis. Of 474 patients eligible for the daratumumab target trial, 136 (28.7%) received daratumumab. Daratumumab was not associated with kidney recovery at 90 days (OR 1.46, 95% CI: 0.84-2.55). Thus, in this multicenter cohort study, neither PLEX nor daratumumab was associated with kidney recovery at 90 days.

papers.t: Supportive Care in Multiple Myeloma: Evidence-Based Recommendations From the Intergroupe Francophone du Myélome (IFM)
papers.a: IFM Supportive Care Working Group et al.
papers.c: By consolidating these 7 domains into a single framework applicable across all lines of therapy, from first-line treatment to relapsed/refractory disease, this review offers a pragmatic reference intended to standardize and improve supportive care and, ultimately, patient outcomes and health-related quality of life in MM. Positions that deliberately differ from other international guidelines-notably those of the International Myeloma Working Group-are explicitly identified and justified.
ab: Multiple myeloma (MM) is a largely incurable plasma cell malignancy in which disease- and treatment-related complications substantially impair quality of life and survival, making supportive care a central determinant of outcome. This review presents unified, evidence-based recommendations from the Intergroupe Francophone du Myélome across 7 domains of supportive care and their implications for contemporary practice, including the era of T-cell-redirecting immunotherapy. With the advent of highly effective induction regimens, autologous stem cell transplantation, immunomodulatory drugs, proteasome inhibitors, anti-CD38 monoclonal antibodies, bispecific antibodies (BsAbs), and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapies, the prevention and management of treatment-emergent toxicities and disease-related sequelae have become increasingly complex. Synthesizing a structured review of the literature, international guidelines, and formal expert consensus, we provide practical recommendations for (1) venous thromboembolism prophylaxis, (2) prevention of skeletal-related events with bone-modifying agents, (3) prevention of infectious complications, (4) vaccination, (5) management of MM-related anemia with erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, (6) adapted physical activity, and (7) practical guidance for the management of treatment-emergent peripheral neuropathy, with particular attention to the specific challenges introduced by BsAbs and CAR-T therapy. By consolidating these 7 domains into a single framework applicable across all lines of therapy, from first-line treatment to relapsed/refractory disease, this review offers a pragmatic reference intended to standardize and improve supportive care and, ultimately, patient outcomes and health-related quality of life in MM. Positions that deliberately differ from other international guidelines-notably those of the International Myeloma Working Group-are explicitly identified and justified.
